blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that addresses the problem of Simpson's paradox in social data analysis, where aggregated trends can mislead by hiding underlying subgroup patterns. The authors propose a method to systematically detect Simpson's paradoxes by examining trends in outcome variables (Y) as a function of independent variables (X), and checking if these trends reverse when data is disaggregated by conditioning on another variable (Z). The paper demonstrates this method using Stack Exchange data, revealing paradoxes such as the counterintuitive trend where later answers in a user's session appear more likely to be accepted as best, which reverses when disaggregated by session length due to survivorship bias. The authors argue that Simpson's paradox often indicates meaningful subgroup differences in social data, and their method can help researchers avoid incorrect inferences and uncover hidden insights.
paper_title: Can you trust the trend? Discovering Simpson’s paradoxes in social data
paper_abstract: arXiv:1801.04385v1 [cs.CY] 13 Jan 2018 Kristina Lerman We investigate how Simpson’s paradox affects analysis of trends in social data. According to the paradox, the trends observed in data that has been aggregated over an entire population may be different from, and even opposite to, those of the underlying subgroups. Failure to take this effect into account can lead analysis to wrong conclusions. We present a statistical method to automatically identify Simpson’s paradox in data by comparing statistical trends in the aggregate data to those in the disaggregated subgroups. We apply the approach to data from Stack Exchange, a popular question-answering platform, to analyze factors affecting answerer performance, specifically, the likelihood that an answer written by a user will be accepted by the asker as the best answer to his or her question. Our analysis confirms a known Simpson’s paradox and identifies several new instances. These paradoxes provide novel insights into user behavior on Stack Exchange. DOI: 10.1145/3159652.3159684 We describe a method to identify Simpson’s paradoxes in the analysis of trends in social data. Our statistical approach finds pairs of variables—that we call Simpson’s pairs—such that a trend in some outcome as a function of the first independent variable observed in the aggregate data disappears or reverses itself when the data is disaggregated into distinct subgroups on the second conditioning variable. We perform mathematical analysis, which identifies two necessary conditions for the paradox to occur: (1) the independent and conditioning variables are correlated and (2) the value of the outcome variable differs within conditioning subgroups. We apply the proposed approach to data collected from Stack Exchange, a popular question-answering platform.
